questions.stem: Two spheres of the same material, with radii $a$ and $b$, fall through the same viscous liquid. If their terminal speeds are $v_a$ and $v_b$, respectively, what is $v_a:v_b$?
questions.solution:
By Stokes’ law, for spheres of the same material falling through the same liquid, terminal speed varies as the square of the radius:
$$v_T\propto r^2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad v_a:v_b=a^2:b^2$$

questions.stem: For the cycle shown, the gas is monatomic and ideal. What are the net work done by the gas over the full cycle and the heat absorbed during $A\to B$?
questions.solution:
For a complete cycle, $W_{\rm cycle}=W_{AB}+W_{BC}+W_{CA}$, with $W_{AB}=100(2-1)=100\,\text{J}$, $W_{BC}=200\ln(1/2)=-200\ln2\,\text{J}$, and $W_{CA}=0$.
$$W_{\rm cycle}=100-200\ln2\,\text{J}$$
For a monatomic ideal gas, $\Delta U_{AB}=\frac32\Delta(PV)=150\,\text{J}$, so $Q_{AB}=\Delta U_{AB}+W_{AB}=250\,\text{J}$. Thus the result is $(100-200\ln2,\ 250)\,\text{J}$.

questions.stem: A particle of mass $3\ \text{kg}$ has position vector $\vec r=(\hat i+2\hat j)\ \text{m}$ relative to a fixed point O at $t=0$, and moves with constant velocity $\vec v=(2\hat i-\hat j+2\hat k)\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Which option gives its angular momentum about O and its time dependence?

options.text: $\vec L=(12\hat i-6\hat j-15\hat k)\ \text{kg m}^2\text{s}^{-1}$, with magnitude $9\sqrt5\ \text{kg m}^2\text{s}^{-1}$; its magnitude changes along the path.
$\vec L=(-12\hat i+6\hat j+15\hat k)\ \text{kg m}^2\text{s}^{-1}$, with magnitude $9\sqrt5\ \text{kg m}^2\text{s}^{-1}$; it remains constant.
$\vec L=(12\hat i-6\hat j+15\hat k)\ \text{kg m}^2\text{s}^{-1}$, with magnitude $9\sqrt5\ \text{kg m}^2\text{s}^{-1}$; it remains constant.
$\vec L=(12\hat i-6\hat j-15\hat k)\ \text{kg m}^2\text{s}^{-1}$, with magnitude $9\sqrt5\ \text{kg m}^2\text{s}^{-1}$; it remains constant.

questions.solution:
Angular momentum is $\vec L=\vec r\times m\vec v$. Thus
$$\vec L=(\hat i+2\hat j)\times(6\hat i-3\hat j+6\hat k)=12\hat i-6\hat j-15\hat k,$$
with $|\vec L|=\sqrt{12^2+(-6)^2+(-15)^2}=9\sqrt5$. Since $\dfrac{d\vec L}{dt}=\vec v\times m\vec v=0$, it remains constant; hence (D).

questions.stem: A sinusoidal wave is described by $y=0.02\sin\left(2\pi t-\dfrac{\pi x}{2}\right)$, where $x$ and $y$ are in metres and $t$ is in seconds. Which set gives its amplitude, wavelength, frequency and speed?
questions.solution:
Comparing with $y=A\sin(\omega t-kx)$ gives $A=0.02$ m, $\omega=2\pi$ rad s$^{-1}$ and $k=\frac{\pi}{2}$ rad m$^{-1}$. Thus
$$f=\frac{\omega}{2\pi}=1\text{ Hz},\quad \lambda=\frac{2\pi}{k}=4\text{ m},\quad v=f\lambda=4\text{ m s}^{-1}.$$
Hence the set is $0.02$ m, $4$ m, $1$ Hz and $4$ m s$^{-1}$.

questions.stem: Masses of $2$ kg and $3$ kg are connected by a light string passing over a frictionless pulley. Taking $g=10$ m s$^{-2}$, what are the acceleration magnitude and string tension?
questions.solution:
For an Atwood machine, $a=\dfrac{(m_2-m_1)g}{m_1+m_2}$.
$$a=\dfrac{(3-2)10}{3+2}=2\ \text{m s}^{-2}$$
For the $2$ kg mass, $T-2g=2a$, so $T=2(10+2)=24\ \text{N}$.

questions.stem: A series LCR circuit has $R=2\ \Omega$, $L=\dfrac{1}{50\pi}$ H and $C=\dfrac{1}{100\pi}$ F. It is connected to a $10$ V rms source of frequency $50$ Hz. What is the impedance?
questions.solution:
For a series LCR circuit, $Z=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}$, where $X_L=2\pi fL=2\,\Omega$ and $X_C=\dfrac{1}{2\pi fC}=1\,\Omega$.
$$Z=\sqrt{2^2+(2-1)^2}=\sqrt{5}\,\Omega$$

questions.stem: Two thin prisms are oppositely oriented. Their yellow-light refractive indices are $\mu_A=1.5$ and $\mu_B=1.6$, and their dispersive powers are $\omega_A=0.04$ and $\omega_B=0.02$, where $\omega=(\mu_v-\mu_r)/(\mu_y-1)$. If the mean deviation is zero and the net violet–red angular separation is $0.04^\circ$, what are their apex angles $A_A$ and $A_B$?
questions.solution:
For a thin prism, mean deviation is $(\mu_y-1)A$. Zero net mean deviation gives
$$0.5A_A=0.6A_B,\qquad A_B=\frac{5}{6}A_A.$$
The net violet–red separation is $|\omega_A(0.5A_A)-\omega_B(0.6A_B)|=0.01A_A=0.04^\circ$, so $A_A=4^\circ$ and $A_B=\frac{10}{3}^\circ$.

questions.stem: In the circuit shown, assume the silicon diode has a constant forward voltage drop of $0.70\ \text{V}$. What power is dissipated in the diode?
questions.solution:
For a forward-biased diode, $I=(10-0.70)/(1.0\ \text{k}\Omega)=9.3\ \text{mA}$. Thus,
$$P_D=V_DI=(0.70)(9.3\ \text{mA})=6.51\ \text{mW}$$

questions.stem: In a YDSE, coherent light gives individual slit intensities $4I_0$ and $I_0$. For $\lambda=600\ \text{nm}$, $d=0.60\ \text{mm}$, $D=1.2\ \text{m}$ and $y=0.45\ \text{mm}$, find $I(y)/I_{\max}$ using the small-angle approximation.
questions.solution:
For two coherent slits, $I=I_1+I_2+2\sqrt{I_1I_2}\cos\phi$, with $\phi=2\pi dy/(\lambda D)=3\pi/4$.
$$\frac{I(y)}{I_{\max}}=\frac{4I_0+I_0+4I_0\cos(3\pi/4)}{(2\sqrt{I_0}+\sqrt{I_0})^2}=\frac{5-2\sqrt{2}}{9}$$

questions.stem: A uniform spring of length $L$ and force constant $k$ is cut into pieces of lengths $L/3$ and $2L/3$. With the same mass attached, the pieces are connected first in series and then in parallel, with their other ends fixed. Find $T_{\text{series}}/T_{\text{parallel}}$.
questions.solution:
For a uniform spring, stiffness is inversely proportional to length, so $k_1=3k$ and $k_2=3k/2$.
$$k_s=\left(\frac1{k_1}+\frac1{k_2}\right)^{-1}=k,\qquad k_p=k_1+k_2=\frac{9k}{2}$$
Since $T=2\pi\sqrt{m/k_{\text{eff}}}$, $
\frac{T_{\text{series}}}{T_{\text{parallel}}}=\sqrt{\frac{k_p}{k_s}}=\boxed{\frac{3}{\sqrt2}}$.

questions.stem: For a metal, light of wavelengths $400\ \text{nm}$ and $800\ \text{nm}$ gives stopping potentials in the ratio $3:1$. Taking $hc=1240\ \text{eV}\cdot\text{nm}$, find the work function of the metal.
questions.solution:
By Einstein’s photoelectric equation, $K_{\text{max}}=hc/\lambda-\phi$, and stopping potential is proportional to $K_{\text{max}}$.
$$\frac{3.10-\phi}{1.55-\phi}=3\quad\Rightarrow\quad \phi=0.775\ \text{eV}$$

questions.stem: A long straight wire carries a uniform charge per unit length of $5.56\times10^{-9}$ C m$^{-1}$. Find the electric field at a distance of $0.10$ m from it. Take $\varepsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12}$ C$^2$ N$^{-1}$ m$^{-2}$.
questions.solution:
By Gauss’s law for a long straight charged wire,
$$E=\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}=\frac{5.56\times10^{-9}}{2\pi(8.85\times10^{-12})(0.10)}\approx 1000\ \text{N C}^{-1}.$$

questions.stem: For two binary inputs, let $+$ denote OR, juxtaposition denote AND, and an overbar denote NOT. A four-gate network is defined by $G_1=\overline{AB}$, $G_2=\overline{A+B}$, $G_3=\overline{G_1G_1}$ and $Y=G_2+G_3$. Which standard gate is equivalent to the network?
questions.solution:
By De Morgan’s law, $G_3=\overline{G_1}=AB$ and $G_2=\overline{A}\,\overline{B}$.
$$Y=AB+\overline{A}\,\overline{B}$$
This is 1 when the inputs are equal, so the network is XNOR.

questions.stem: Two fixed charges $+9q$ and $+4q$ are held $20$ cm apart, where $q>0$. A charge $-q$ is free to move between them. At what distance from $+9q$ is its net force zero?
questions.solution:
For zero net force, the attractive force magnitudes must be equal. If $x$ is the distance from $+9q$,
$$\frac{9}{x^2}=\frac{4}{(20-x)^2}\Rightarrow \frac{3}{x}=\frac{2}{20-x}\Rightarrow x=12\text{ cm}.$$

questions.stem: A concave mirror forms real, inverted images. When an object is moved $8$ cm towards it, the image size changes from $3$ times to $5$ times the object size. What is the image distance in the second position?
questions.solution:
For a real image, $|m|=v/u$ and the mirror formula gives $u=\frac{(m-1)f}{m}$. Thus $u_1=\frac{4f}{3}$ and $u_2=\frac{6f}{5}$; since the object moves $8$ cm toward the mirror, $\frac{4f}{3}-\frac{6f}{5}=8$, giving $f=60$ cm.
In the second position, $v_2=5u_2=6f=360$ cm.

questions.stem: A body is projected radially upward from the surface of a spherical planet of mass $M$ and radius $R$ with speed $\sqrt{\dfrac{3GM}{2R}}$. Neglect the atmosphere. What maximum height above the surface does it reach?
questions.solution:
By conservation of mechanical energy, at the maximum height the speed is zero:
$$\frac{v_0^2}{2}-\frac{GM}{R}=-\frac{GM}{R+h}$$
Substituting $v_0^2=\frac{3GM}{2R}$ gives $R+h=4R$, hence $h=3R$.

questions.stem: An $\alpha$ particle starts from rest and is accelerated through a potential difference of $100$ V. Calculate its de Broglie wavelength. Take $h=6.63\times10^{-34}$ J s, $m_\alpha=6.64\times10^{-27}$ kg and $e=1.60\times10^{-19}$ C.
questions.solution:
For an $\alpha$ particle, $q=2e$ and $K=qV$. Hence
$$\lambda=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2m_\alpha qV}}=\frac{6.63\times10^{-34}}{\sqrt{2(6.64\times10^{-27})(3.20\times10^{-19})(100)}}=1.02\times10^{-12}\text{ m}.$$

questions.stem: A plane electromagnetic wave of intensity $900$ W m$^{-2}$ is incident normally on a perfectly reflecting mirror of area $0.50$ m$^2$. Taking $c=3.0\times10^8$ m s$^{-1}$, what force does the wave exert on the mirror?
questions.solution:
For a perfectly reflecting mirror at normal incidence, radiation pressure is $p=\dfrac{2I}{c}$.
$$F=pA=\frac{2IA}{c}=\frac{2(900)(0.50)}{3.0\times10^8}=3.0\times10^{-6}\ \text{N}$$
questions.subtopic: Radiation pressure / momentum of EM waves

questions.stem: A regular hexagonal wire loop and a circular wire loop are concentric and coplanar, with circumradius and radius respectively both $0.12$ m. Each carries $6$ A, in opposite senses. Find the magnitude of the net magnetic field at the centre. Take $\mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \text{T m A}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
For a regular $n$-sided loop of circumradius $R$, $B_n=\dfrac{\mu_0 I n}{2\pi R}\tan\dfrac{\pi}{n}$. Thus, for the hexagon and circle,
$$B_h=2\sqrt{3}\times10^{-5}\ \text{T},\qquad B_c=\pi\times10^{-5}\ \text{T}.$$
Their fields oppose, so $B_{\rm net}=|B_h-B_c|=(2\sqrt{3}-\pi)\times10^{-5}\ \text{T}$.
questions.subtopic: Magnetic field due to finite wire / polygon loop

questions.stem: Four point masses of $1$ kg, $2$ kg, $3$ kg and $4$ kg are placed at the four corners of a square of side $2$ m. Find their moment of inertia about an axis through the square's centre and perpendicular to its plane.
questions.solution:
Each corner is at squared distance $r^2=\frac{2^2}{2}=2\,\text{m}^2$ from the axis. Using $I=\sum mr^2$,
$$I=(1+2+3+4)(2)=20\,\text{kg m}^2$$
questions.subtopic: Moment of inertia of point masses

questions.stem: A projectile has trajectory $y=\dfrac34x-\dfrac{5}{64}x^2$, with $x$ and $y$ measured in metres. Taking $g=10$ m s$^{-2}$, its launch speed, projection angle and horizontal range are:
questions.solution: For a projectile, $y=x\tan\theta-\dfrac{g x^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta}$. Comparing coefficients gives $\tan\theta=\dfrac34$ and $\dfrac{10}{2u^2(16/25)}=\dfrac{5}{64}$, hence $u=10\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. The range is the nonzero root of $y=0$: $R=\dfrac{3/4}{5/64}=\dfrac{48}{5}\ \text{m}$.

questions.stem: For a dilute ideal gas of fixed-diameter hard-sphere molecules, let $n$ be number density, $\lambda$ mean free path and $\tau=\lambda/\bar v$ mean free time. For a fixed amount of gas, which statements are correct? (i) $\lambda\propto\dfrac{1}{nd^2}$. (ii) At constant pressure, $\lambda\propto T$. (iii) At constant volume, $\tau\propto T^{-1/2}$. (iv) At constant pressure, $\tau$ is independent of $T$.
questions.solution:
For hard spheres, $
$$\lambda=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}\pi nd^2},\qquad \tau=\frac{\lambda}{\bar v}\propto\frac{1}{n\sqrt T}.\u000a$$At constant pressure, $$n\propto T^{-1}$$, hence $$\lambda\propto T$$ and $$\tau\propto T^{1/2}$$; at constant volume, $n$ is constant, so $$\tau\propto$ T^{-1/2}$. Thus (i), (ii) and (iii) are correct.
questions.subtopic: Mean free path / mean free time

questions.stem: A wire has resistance $4\ \Omega$. It is stretched until its length is three times its original length, with its volume unchanged. What is its new resistance?
questions.solution:
With volume constant, $A'L'=AL$. Thus $L'=3L$ and $A'=A/3$.
$$R'=\rho\frac{L'}{A'}=9R=9(4)=36\ \Omega$$

questions.stem: A thermometer X reads $10$ °X at $0$ °C and $160$ °X at $100$ °C. At what Celsius temperature do the two thermometers show the same numerical reading?
questions.solution:
The thermometer scale is linear, so $X=10+\frac{160-10}{100}C=10+1.5C$.
Setting the readings equal, $X=C$:
$$C=10+1.5C\implies C=-20^\circ\text{C}.$$

questions.stem: Two bodies A and B have masses $m$ and $4m$ and equal momenta. What is the ratio of their kinetic energies, $K_A:K_B$?
questions.solution:
For equal momentum, $K=\dfrac{p^2}{2m}$, so kinetic energy is inversely proportional to mass.
$$K_A:K_B=\frac{1}{m}:\frac{1}{4m}=4:1$$

questions.stem: A source emitting frequency $f_0$ moves at $120$ m s$^{-1}$ along a straight track past a stationary observer. A uniform wind blows along the track in the source’s direction at $60$ m s$^{-1}$; sound speed relative to air is $300$ m s$^{-1}$. What is the ratio of the observed frequency while approaching to that while receding?
questions.solution:
With wind speed $w$ along the source’s motion, the sound speeds along and against the wind are $c+w=360$ and $c-w=240$ m s$^{-1}$.
$$\frac{f_{\rm app}}{f_{\rm rec}}=\frac{(c+w)/(c+w-v)}{(c-w)/(c-w+v)}=\frac{360/240}{240/360}=\frac94$$

questions.stem: A capacitor of capacitance $5$ μF is connected across a $12$ V battery. How much energy is stored in it?
questions.solution:
The energy stored in a capacitor is $U=\frac12 CV^2$.
$$U=\frac12(5\times10^{-6})(12)^2=3.6\times10^{-4}\ \text{J}$$

questions.stem: Monochromatic light of wavelength $500$ nm produces the single-slit diffraction pattern shown. What is the slit width?
questions.solution:
For the first minimum in single-slit diffraction, $a\sin\theta=\lambda$.
$$a=\frac{500\ \text{nm}}{\sin30^\circ}=1000\ \text{nm}=1.00\ \mu\text{m}$$

questions.stem: The atomic masses of $^{49}_{26}\text{X}$ and $^{48}_{26}\text{X}$ are $48.954918$ u and $47.952253$ u, respectively. Given $m_n=1.008665$ u and $1\ \text{u}c^2=931.5$ MeV, find the neutron separation energy. Take $m_e=0.000549$ u.
questions.solution:
The neutron separation energy is $S_n=[M(^{48}_{26}\text{X})+m_n-M(^{49}_{26}\text{X})]c^2$; the equal electron masses in the atomic masses cancel.
$$S_n=[47.952253+1.008665-48.954918](931.5)=5.589\ \text{MeV}$$

questions.stem: Two wires are separately stretched by the same tensile force. Wire A has length $1.5$ m, diameter $2.0$ mm and Young's modulus $2.0\times10^{11}$ Pa; wire B has length $1.0$ m and Young's modulus $3.0\times10^{11}$ Pa. If their elongations are equal, find the diameter of wire B.
questions.solution:
For a wire, $\Delta L=\dfrac{4FL}{\pi Yd^2}$. Equal elongations under the same force give
$$d_B^2=d_A^2\frac{L_BY_A}{L_AY_B}=(2.0)^2\frac{1.0(2.0)}{1.5(3.0)}=\frac{16}{9}\text{ mm}^2.$$
Thus, $d_B=\dfrac{4}{3}\text{ mm}$.

questions.stem: A solid cylinder has measured mass $(200.0\pm2.0)$ g, diameter $(4.00\pm0.08)$ cm and height $(10.0\pm0.15)$ cm. Using maximum-error propagation, what is the percentage error in its density?
questions.solution:
For $\rho=\dfrac{4m}{\pi d^2h}$, the maximum fractional error is $\dfrac{\Delta m}{m}+2\dfrac{\Delta d}{d}+\dfrac{\Delta h}{h}$.
$$\%\text{ error}=1\%+2(2\%)+1.5\%=6.5\%$$

questions.stem: An ideal series LR circuit with $L=2\ \text{H}$ and $R=4\ \Omega$ is connected to a $12\ \text{V}$ battery at $t=0$. At what time does the current reach $75\%$ of its steady value?
questions.solution:
For a series LR circuit, $\dfrac{i}{I_{\max}}=1-e^{-Rt/L}$. Setting $i/I_{\max}=3/4$ gives
$$e^{-Rt/L}=\frac14,\qquad t=\frac{L}{R}\ln 4=\frac{2}{4}\ln 4=\ln 2\ \text{s}.$$

questions.stem: For the velocity–time graph shown, find the particle's displacement and distance travelled, respectively, during the interval shown.
questions.solution:
Displacement is the signed area under the velocity–time graph; distance is the sum of the absolute areas. Thus,
$$\Delta x=28.5-5.5=23\ \text{m},\qquad s=28.5+5.5=34\ \text{m}$$

questions.stem: A hydrogen-like ion has ground-state ionization energy $54.4\ \text{eV}$. Starting in its ground state, it absorbs a $51.0\ \text{eV}$ photon. Find the principal quantum number reached and the maximum number of distinct emission lines possible in its subsequent de-excitation.
questions.solution:
For absorption from the ground state, $54.4\left(1-\dfrac{1}{n^2}\right)=51.0$, giving $n=4$. The maximum number of distinct emission lines is
$$N=\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}=\dfrac{4\cdot3}{2}=6.$$

questions.stem: Two satellites orbit the same planet in circular orbits of radii $r$ and $4r$. If the satellite at radius $r$ has an orbital period of $6$ h, what is the period of the other satellite?
questions.solution:
For satellites orbiting the same planet, Kepler’s third law gives $T\propto r^{3/2}$.
$$\frac{T_2}{T_1}=\left(\frac{4r}{r}\right)^{3/2}=8$$
Thus, $T_2=8(6)=48\text{ h}$.

questions.stem: A mixture contains monatomic and rigid diatomic ideal gases in mole ratio $2:1$, with vibrational modes inactive. The mixture's molar $C_p$, molar $C_v$, and $\gamma=C_p/C_v$, respectively, are (where $R$ is the molar gas constant):
questions.solution:
For 2 mol monatomic and 1 mol rigid diatomic gas, $C_v$ per mole of mixture is
$$C_v=\frac{2(3R/2)+5R/2}{3}=\frac{11R}{6}.$$
Using $C_p=C_v+R$, $C_p=\frac{17R}{6}$ and $\gamma=\frac{C_p}{C_v}=\frac{17}{11}$.

questions.stem: A charged particle moves helically in a uniform magnetic field, with its initial velocity making an angle $\theta$ with the field. After two complete revolutions, its axial displacement equals the circumference of its circular projection. Find $\theta$.
questions.solution:
The axial displacement in two revolutions is $2v\cos\theta\,T$, while the projected circle’s circumference is $2\pi v\sin\theta/\omega$, with $T=2\pi/\omega$.
$$2v\cos\theta\frac{2\pi}{\omega}=\frac{2\pi v\sin\theta}{\omega}\quad\Rightarrow\quad \tan\theta=2$$
Hence, $\theta=\tan^{-1}(2)$.

questions.stem: Two cells of emfs $12$ V and $4$ V, each with internal resistance $2\ \text{Ω}$, are connected in parallel with like terminals together and a $3\ \text{Ω}$ resistor across the combination. Find $(I_R,I_{4\text{V}})$, taking current outward from a cell’s positive terminal as positive.
questions.solution:
Let $V$ be the common terminal voltage. By KCL,
$$\frac{12-V}{2}+\frac{4-V}{2}=\frac{V}{3}\quad\Rightarrow\quad V=6\text{ V}.$$
Hence $I_R=V/3=2\text{ A}$ and $I_{4\text{V}}=(4-V)/2=-1\text{ A}$, so $(I_R,I_{4\text{V}})=(2,-1)\text{ A}$.

questions.stem: A car moves at $10\sqrt{2}$ m s$^{-1}$ on a banked circular track of radius $20$ m. The banking angle is $30^\circ$. Find the minimum coefficient of static friction needed to prevent slipping. Take $g=10$ m s$^{-2}$.
questions.solution:
Since $v^2/r=10>g\tan30^\circ$, friction acts down the bank. Resolving forces horizontally and vertically gives
$$\mu_s=\frac{(v^2/r)\cos30^\circ-g\sin30^\circ}{g\cos30^\circ+(v^2/r)\sin30^\circ}=\frac{\cos30^\circ-\sin30^\circ}{\cos30^\circ+\sin30^\circ}=2-\sqrt{3}.$$

questions.stem: A $100$ g piece of ice at $0^\circ$C is mixed with $300$ g of water at $40^\circ$C in an insulated vessel of negligible heat capacity. Take $c_{\text{water}}=1\ \text{cal g}^{-1}\, ^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$ and $L_f=80\ \text{cal g}^{-1}$. Find the final temperature.
questions.solution:
Heat released by the warm water cooling to $0^\circ\text{C}$ is $300(1)(40)=12000\ \text{cal}$, while melting the ice requires $100(80)=8000\ \text{cal}$; hence all the ice melts.
$$12000=8000+(300+100)(1)T \quad\Rightarrow\quad T=10^\circ\text{C}$$

questions.stem: Which statement about adsorption is incorrect?

options.text: Physical adsorption is generally favoured by increasing temperature.
For a fixed mass of adsorbent, greater surface area generally increases adsorption.

questions.solution: Physical adsorption is generally exothermic, so increasing temperature shifts equilibrium toward desorption and decreases adsorption. Hence it is not generally favoured by increasing temperature.

questions.stem: A $10.0$ g impure sample containing $80.0\%$ $\text{CaC}_2$ reacts with excess water. The acetylene formed is ignited with $5.60$ L of $\text{O}_2$ at STP. How many moles of $\text{C}_2\text{H}_2$ remain after cooling? Take $M(\text{CaC}_2)=64$ g mol$^{-1}$ and the molar volume at STP as $22.4$ L mol$^{-1}$. Impurities are inert.
questions.solution:
The sample contains $10.0(0.800)=8.00$ g of $\text{CaC}_2$, forming $8.00/64=0.125$ mol of $\text{C}_2\text{H}_2$. Also, $n_{\text{O}_2}=5.60/22.4=0.250$ mol.
$$\text{C}_2\text{H}_2+\frac{5}{2}\text{O}_2\to2\text{CO}_2+\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
Thus $0.250/(5/2)=0.100$ mol of acetylene burns, leaving $0.125-0.100=\boxed{0.0250\text{ mol}}$.

questions.stem: Which isolated ion has three unpaired electrons?
questions.solution: For isolated ions, remove $4s$ electrons before $3d$ electrons. Thus, $\text{V}^{2+}$ has configuration $3d^3$; by Hund’s rule, all three electrons are unpaired.

questions.stem: For equal volumes at the same temperature and pressure, methane effuses in $20$ s and gas X in $30$ s. Find the molar mass of X. Take $M(\text{CH}_4)=16\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
For equal volumes, the effusion time is proportional to the square root of molar mass:
$$\frac{t_X}{t_{\mathrm{CH}_4}}=\sqrt{\frac{M_X}{M_{\mathrm{CH}_4}}}$$
$$M_X=16\left(\frac{30}{20}\right)^2=36\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$$

questions.stem: At $300$ K, $\Delta U=-282.8\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ for $\text{CO}(g)+\dfrac{1}{2}\text{O}_2(g)\to\text{CO}_2(g)$. Given $\Delta H_f^\circ[\text{CO}_2(g)]=-394\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ and $R=8.0\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$, find $\Delta H_f^\circ[\text{CO}(g)]$.
questions.solution:
For gaseous reactions, $\Delta H=\Delta U+\Delta n_gRT$, where $\Delta n_g=1-(1+\frac12)=-\frac12$.
$$\Delta H=-282.8+\frac{(-\frac12)(8.0)(300)}{1000}=-284.0\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$
Using $\Delta H=\Delta H_f^\circ(\text{CO}_2)-\Delta H_f^\circ(\text{CO})$, we get $\Delta H_f^\circ(\text{CO})=-394-(-284)=-110\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

questions.stem: Given $E^\circ_{\text{Ag}^+/\text{Ag}}=0.80\ \text{V}$ and $E^\circ_{\text{Zn}^{2+}/\text{Zn}}=-0.76\ \text{V}$, find $E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$ for $\text{Zn}|\text{Zn}^{2+}||\text{Ag}^+|\text{Ag}$.
questions.solution:
For a galvanic cell, $E^\circ_{\text{cell}}=E^\circ_{\text{cathode}}-E^\circ_{\text{anode}}$. Here, Ag is the cathode and Zn is the anode:
$$E^\circ_{\text{cell}}=0.80-(-0.76)=1.56\ \text{V}$$

questions.stem: Which artificial sweetener is a chlorinated derivative of sucrose?
questions.solution: Sucralose is formed by replacing hydroxyl groups in sucrose with chlorine atoms; hence it is a chlorinated derivative of sucrose.

questions.stem: For lactose, consider the statements: I. Its glycosidic linkage is $\beta(1\to4)$. II. It is a non-reducing disaccharide. III. On hydrolysis, it yields glucose and galactose. Which statements are correct?
questions.solution:
Lactose has a $\eta(1\to4)$ glycosidic linkage and hydrolyses to glucose and galactose. Its free anomeric carbon makes it a reducing disaccharide, so statement II is false.
Thus, statements I and III are correct.

questions.stem: For the octahedral complexes $[\text{Co}(en)_2\text{Cl}_2]^+$ and $[\text{Cr}(ox)_2(\text{NH}_3)_2]^-$, which statement is correct?

options.text: Each has 2 isomers; neither shows optical isomerism.
Each has 3 isomers; the cis form is optically active, while the trans form is not.
Each has 4 isomers; both cis and trans forms are optically active.
Each has 3 isomers; the trans form is optically active, while the cis form is not.

questions.solution:
For octahedral $[M(AA)_2X_2]$, the trans form is achiral, while the cis form exists as a pair of optical isomers ($\Delta$ and $\Lambda$).
Thus, each complex has $1+2=3$ isomers; the cis form is optically active and the trans form is not.

questions.stem: Two first-order reactions, $X$ and $Y$, have the $\ln([C]/[C]_0)$ versus time plots shown in the figure. When $[Y]=[Y]_0/4$, what fraction of its initial concentration remains for $X$?
questions.solution:
For a first-order reaction, $\ln([C]/[C]_0)=-kt$. From the graph, $k_X/k_Y=2$, so when $[Y]/[Y]_0=1/4$,
$$\frac{[X]}{[X]_0}=e^{-k_Xt}=\left(e^{-k_Yt}\right)^2=\left(\frac14\right)^2=\frac{1}{16}.$$

questions.stem: Which set contains species whose central atoms all have the same hybridisation?
questions.solution:
Hybridisation is determined by the number of electron domains around the central atom. In $\text{BF}_3$, $\text{SO}_3$, and $\text{NO}_3^-$, each central atom has three electron domains and trigonal-planar geometry:
$$\text{BF}_3:\ sp^2,\text{ }\text{SO}_3:\ sp^2,\text{ }\text{NO}_3^-:\ sp^2$$

questions.stem: Phenol is converted successively using (i) Zn dust and heat, (ii) $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}/\text{AlCl}_3$, (iii) NBS and $h\nu$, and (iv) $\text{CH}_3\text{ONa}$ in methanol. What is the major final product?
questions.solution:
Zn dust and heat reduce phenol to benzene; Friedel–Crafts methylation gives toluene. NBS and $h\nu$ brominate the benzylic position, followed by substitution with methoxide:
$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3 \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Br} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{OCH}_3$$
The final product is benzyl methyl ether.

questions.stem: The three alkenes below hydrogenate completely to the same alkane. Which sequence gives decreasing magnitude of heat released?
questions.solution:
Alkene stability increases with the degree of substitution: $\text{2-methylbut-2-ene} > \text{2-methylbut-1-ene} > \text{3-methylbut-1-ene}$. Since heat released on hydrogenation varies inversely with alkene stability,
$$|\Delta H|: \text{3-methylbut-1-ene} > \text{2-methylbut-1-ene} > \text{2-methylbut-2-ene}.$$
questions.subtopic: Stability of alkenes / heat of hydrogenation

questions.stem: Given $\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{HCl})=426.0$, $\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3)=238.8$ and $\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{NaCl})=126.4$ $\text{S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}$, find $\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3)$.
questions.solution:
By Kohlrausch’s law, $\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3)=2\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{HCl})+\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3)-2\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{NaCl})$.
$$\Lambda_m^\circ=2(426.0)+238.8-2(126.4)=838.0\ \text{S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}$$

questions.stem: Arrange the following free radicals in decreasing order of stability: $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^\bullet$, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}^\bullet$, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2^\bullet$ and $\text{CH}_3^\bullet$.
questions.solution:
Radical stability increases with alkyl substitution due to hyperconjugation.
$$3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ > \text{methyl}$$

questions.stem: Which sequence gives increasing C–O bond length in the indicated species?
questions.solution:
C–O bond length decreases as bond order increases. The bond orders are $3$ in CO, $2$ in CO₂, and an average of $\dfrac{4}{3}$ in CO₃²⁻; hence bond lengths increase as
$$\text{CO} < \text{CO}_2 < \text{CO}_3^{2-}$$

questions.stem: In a crystalline solid, X ions form an FCC lattice with some X sites vacant; A and B occupy, respectively, one-quarter of the tetrahedral and octahedral voids. Given $a=5.00\ \text{Å}$, $\rho=1.56\ \text{g cm}^{-3}$, $N_{\mathrm{A}}=6.00\times10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$, and $M_A=23$, $M_B=39$, $M_X=16\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$, find the empirical formula.
questions.solution:
An FCC unit cell has 8 tetrahedral and 4 octahedral voids, so $n_A=8(1/4)=2$ and $n_B=4(1/4)=1$.
$$M_{\text{cell}}=\rho a^3N_A=1.56(5.00\times10^{-8})^3(6.00\times10^{23})=117\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$$
Thus, $n_X=[117-2(23)-39]/16=2$. The empirical formula is $\text{A}_2\text{B}\text{X}_2$.

questions.stem: Propyne is treated successively with $\text{NaNH}_2$, $\text{CH}_3\text{I}$ and $\text{HgSO}_4/\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4/\text{H}_2\text{O}$. What is the major final product?
questions.solution:
NaNH₂ deprotonates propyne, and the acetylide ion undergoes alkylation with CH₃I:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{C}\equiv\text{CH}\xrightarrow{\text{NaNH}_2,\,\text{CH}_3\text{I}}\text{CH}_3\text{C}\equiv\text{CCH}_3$$
Hydration of but-2-yne with HgSO₄/H₂SO₄/H₂O gives butan-2-one, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$.

questions.stem: For octahedral complexes I, $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{4-}$; II, $[\text{FeF}_6]^{3-}$; and III, $[\text{CoF}_6]^{3-}$, which option gives, in order, the number of unpaired electrons, orbital CFSE (excluding pairing energy), and spin-only magnetic moment?
questions.solution:
I: Fe²⁺ is low-spin d⁶, so $t_{2g}^6$ gives $n=0$ and CFSE $=-2.4\Delta_o$. II: Fe³⁺ is high-spin d⁵, so $t_{2g}^3e_g^2$ gives $n=5$ and CFSE $=0$.
III: Co³⁺ is high-spin d⁶, so $t_{2g}^4e_g^2$ gives $n=4$ and CFSE $=-0.4\Delta_o$. Using $\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}\,\text{BM}$ gives $0$, $\sqrt{35}$, and $\sqrt{24}$ BM, respectively.

questions.stem: Which reagent sequence converts nitrobenzene into 4-hydroxyazobenzene through benzenediazonium chloride?
questions.solution:
Sn/HCl reduces nitrobenzene to aniline; NaOH liberates the free amine. Diazotisation at $0$–$5^\circ\text{C}$ forms benzenediazonium chloride, which couples with phenol in cold alkaline medium at the para position.
$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NO}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Sn/HCl, then NaOH}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{NaNO}_2/\text{HCl},\ 0\text{–}5^\circ\text{C}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^- \xrightarrow{\text{phenol/NaOH, cold}} \text{4-hydroxyazobenzene}$$

questions.stem: Which statement is correct for a process at constant temperature and pressure?

options.text: A process with $\Delta G>0$ is spontaneous in the forward direction.
A process with $\Delta H>0$ can never be spontaneous.
A process with $\Delta G<0$ is spontaneous in the forward direction.

questions.solution:
At constant temperature and pressure, a process is spontaneous in the forward direction when
$$\Delta G<0.$$
At equilibrium, $\Delta G=0$, while $\Delta H>0$ does not rule out spontaneity.

questions.stem: According to VSEPR theory, what are the number of lone pairs on xenon and the shape of $\text{XeF}_4$?
questions.solution:
Xenon has $8$ valence electrons; after forming four Xe–F bonds, it has two lone pairs.
For $\text{XeF}_4$, the six electron pairs are octahedrally arranged, with the two lone pairs opposite each other, giving a square-planar shape.

questions.stem: Which is the decreasing order of SN1 reactivity?
questions.solution:
SN1 reactivity follows carbocation stability. The allylic carbocation formed from 3-chlorobut-1-ene is resonance-stabilised, while 2-chlorobutane forms a secondary carbocation and 1-chlorobutane a primary one.
$$\text{3-Chlorobut-1-ene} > \text{2-chlorobutane} > \text{1-chlorobutane}$$

questions.stem: Which is the decreasing order of stability of the following carbanions?

options.text: Ethyl anion > allyl anion > cyclopentadienyl anion
Allyl anion > cyclopentadienyl anion > ethyl anion
Cyclopentadienyl anion > allyl anion > ethyl anion
Cyclopentadienyl anion > ethyl anion > allyl anion

questions.solution:
The cyclopentadienyl anion is aromatic with $6\pi$ electrons; the allyl anion is resonance-stabilised, while the ethyl anion has no resonance stabilisation. Hence, stability decreases as
$$\text{cyclopentadienyl anion} > \text{allyl anion} > \text{ethyl anion}.$$

questions.stem:
Evaluate the statements about amino acids:
I. Near its isoelectric pH, an amino acid is predominantly a zwitterion.
II. For an amino acid with a non-ionisable side chain, its net charge is positive below its isoelectric pH and negative above it.
III. Every amino acid used in protein synthesis must be obtained from the diet.
IV. A peptide bond can form between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of another, with elimination of water.
Which set is correct?
questions.solution:
At the isoelectric pH, amino acids predominantly exist as zwitterions; below it they carry a net positive charge and above it, a net negative charge.
Not all amino acids must be obtained from the diet, since the body synthesizes nonessential amino acids.
Peptide bonds form by condensation between the carboxyl and amino groups, eliminating water. Thus I, II and IV are true.

questions.stem: For nitrosation of the phenol shown in the figure, which is the major mononitroso product?
questions.solution: ${-OH}$ directs electrophilic substitution to the ortho and para positions. The para position is less hindered than the available ortho position, so nitrosation gives 4-nitroso-2-methylphenol as the major product.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the bonding in diborane, $\text{B}_2\text{H}_6$?

options.text: It contains ionic B–H bonds formed by complete electron transfer.
It contains only ordinary two-centre, two-electron bonds.
It contains two three-centre, two-electron B–H–B bonds.
It contains two three-centre, four-electron B–H–B bonds.

questions.solution: Diborane has four terminal B–H two-centre bonds and two bridging B–H–B bonds. Each bridge is a three-centre, two-electron bond (3c–2e).

questions.stem: Pure $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4(g)$ dissociates as $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4(g)\rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}_2(g)$. At equilibrium, its degree of dissociation is $0.50$ and the total pressure is $3.0$ atm. Using pressures in atm, find $K_p$.
questions.solution:
For 1 mol of N₂O₄ initially, equilibrium amounts are 0.50 mol N₂O₄ and 1.00 mol NO₂, so their partial pressures are 1.0 atm and 2.0 atm.
$$K_p=\frac{p_{\mathrm{NO_2}}^2}{p_{\mathrm{N_2O_4}}}=\frac{(2.0)^2}{1.0}=4.0\ \text{atm}$$

questions.stem: 4-Methylbenzaldehyde is treated with concentrated aqueous $\text{NaOH}$, followed by acidification. Which pair of organic products is formed?
questions.solution:
4-Methylbenzaldehyde has no $\alpha$-hydrogen, so it undergoes the Cannizzaro reaction.
$$2\,\text{ArCHO}+\text{OH}^-\rightarrow\text{ArCH}_2\text{OH}+\text{ArCOO}^-$$
Acidification converts $\text{ArCOO}^-$ to $\text{ArCOOH}$, giving 4-methylbenzyl alcohol and 4-methylbenzoic acid.

questions.stem: Which statement about photochemical smog and ozone depletion is incorrect?

options.text: Peroxyacetyl nitrate is an eye irritant found in photochemical smog.
Photolysis of $\text{NO}_2$ can lead to the formation of ozone in the troposphere.
Photochemical smog forms most readily under cool, cloudy conditions.
Chlorine radicals released from CFCs can catalytically destroy stratospheric ozone.

questions.solution: Photochemical smog forms most readily in warm, sunny conditions with stagnant air, as sunlight drives the reactions. Hence the statement that it forms under cool, cloudy conditions is incorrect.

questions.stem: To prepare 2-ethoxy-2-methylpropane from 2-methylpropan-2-ol, which reagent sequence is most suitable?
questions.solution:
Sodium converts 2-methylpropan-2-ol into sodium tert-butoxide, which forms the ether by Williamson synthesis with ethyl bromide:
$$ (CH_3)_3COH \xrightarrow{Na} (CH_3)_3CONa \xrightarrow{C_2H_5Br} (CH_3)_3COC_2H_5 $$
Hence, the suitable sequence is $Na$, then $C_2H_5Br$.

questions.stem: For the equilibria $\text{H}_2(g)+\text{Cl}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{HCl}(g)$, $K_1=2$; $2\text{HCl}(g)+\dfrac12\text{O}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)+\text{Cl}_2(g)$, $K_2=4$; and $2\text{O}(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{O}_2(g)$, $K_3=64$, find $K$ for $2\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)+2\text{O}(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{H}_2(g)+2\text{O}_2(g)$. All equilibrium constants are dimensionless.
questions.solution:
Add reactions 1 and 2 to obtain $\text{H}_2+\frac12\text{O}_2\rightleftharpoons\text{H}_2\text{O}$, with $K=K_1K_2=8$. Reverse and double this reaction, then add reaction 3:
$$K=(K_1K_2)^{-2}K_3=8^{-2}\times64=1.$$

questions.stem: What is the ratio of the energy of a photon emitted by $\text{He}^+$ in the transition $n=3\to2$ to that emitted by hydrogen in the transition $n=4\to2$?
questions.solution:
For a hydrogen-like species, $E\propto Z^2\left(\frac{1}{n_f^2}-\frac{1}{n_i^2}\right)$. Thus,
$$\frac{E_{\text{He}^+}}{E_{\text{H}}}=\frac{4\left(\frac14-\frac19\right)}{\frac14-\frac1{16}}=\frac{80}{27}$$

questions.stem: Which pairing of an aqueous transition-metal ion with its characteristic colour is correct?
questions.solution:
Aqueous $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ions are characteristically blue due to $d$–$d$ transitions.
Thus, the correct pairing is $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ — blue.

questions.stem: The products formed when $\text{PCl}_5$ undergoes complete hydrolysis in excess water are:
questions.solution:
Complete hydrolysis of $\text{PCl}_5$ produces phosphoric acid and hydrogen chloride:
$$\text{PCl}_5+4\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightarrow\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4+5\text{HCl}$$
Thus, the products are $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$ and $\text{HCl}$.

questions.stem: On heating $\text{CaCO}_3$, it forms $X+Y$; $X$ reacts with water to give $Z$, and limited $\text{CO}_2$ converts $Z$ to $W$. Identify $X,Y,Z,W$.
questions.solution:
On heating, calcium carbonate undergoes thermal decomposition:
$$\text{CaCO}_3 \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} \text{CaO}+\text{CO}_2$$
Then $\text{CaO}+\text{H}_2\text{O}\to\text{Ca(OH)}_2$, and limited $\text{CO}_2$ gives $\text{Ca(OH)}_2+\text{CO}_2\to\text{CaCO}_3+\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Thus $X=\text{CaO},\ Y=\text{CO}_2,\ Z=\text{Ca(OH)}_2,\ W=\text{CaCO}_3$..

questions.stem: For the transition shown in the figure, find $(\Delta E_{\text{em}}/13.6\ \text{eV},\ r_4/a_0)$ for $\text{Li}^{2+}$. Use $E_n=-13.6Z^2/n^2$ eV and $r_n=a_0n^2/Z$.
questions.solution:
For Li$^{2+}$, $Z=3$ and the transition is $n=4\to2$.
$$\frac{\Delta E_{\text{em}}}{13.6\ \text{eV}}=Z^2\left(\frac{1}{2^2}-\frac{1}{4^2}\right)=\frac{27}{16}$$
$$\frac{r_4}{a_0}=\frac{4^2}{3}=\frac{16}{3}$$

questions.stem: 1-Bromobutane is heated with alcoholic $\text{KOH}$; the alkene formed is treated with $\text{HBr}$ in peroxide, then with $\text{NaI}$ in acetone. What is the final product?
questions.solution:
Alcoholic KOH causes elimination, and peroxide-assisted HBr addition is anti-Markovnikov:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} \xrightarrow{\text{alc. KOH},\ \Delta} \text{CH}_2{=}\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3 \xrightarrow{\text{HBr}/\text{peroxide}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$$
NaI in acetone replaces Br with I, giving 1-iodobutane.

questions.stem: For the elements $\text{Na}$, $\text{Mg}$, $\text{Al}$ and $\text{Si}$, which stated order is incorrect?
questions.solution:
Across period 3, the magnitude of electron gain enthalpy is approximately Si: $134$, Na: $53$, Al: $44$, and Mg: $0$ kJ mol$^{-1}$.
Thus, the correct order is $\text{Si} > \text{Na} > \text{Al} > \text{Mg}$; the stated order incorrectly places Al above Na.

questions.stem: Assuming complete dissociation, what is the boiling-point elevation of a $0.20\ \text{mol kg}^{-1}$ solution of $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{Cl}]\text{Cl}_2$ in water? Take $K_b=0.52\ \text{K kg mol}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
On complete dissociation, $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{Cl}]\text{Cl}_2$ produces $3$ ions, so $i=3$.
$$\Delta T_b=iK_bm=3(0.52)(0.20)=0.312\ \text{K}$$

questions.stem:
Find the part of the sentence which contains an error.

(a) Each of the measures announced by the central bank / (b) to curb inflation / (c) has been reviewed by the finance ministry / (d) No error

options.text: Each of the measures announced by the central bank
has been reviewed by the finance ministry

questions.solution: “Each” takes a singular verb, so “has been reviewed” is correct. The other parts are grammatically sound; hence there is no error.

questions.stem: The historian's refusal to label the rebel either a hero or a traitor was not ___ but ___: she distinguished documented motives from later political mythmaking.
questions.solution: The distinction between documented motives and political mythmaking shows careful, evidence-based fairness, not evasive ambiguity. Thus, the words are “equivocation” and “scrupulous impartiality.”

questions.stem: Choose the word nearest in meaning to **apocryphal**.
questions.solution: “Apocryphal” means of doubtful authenticity or false; “spurious” means not genuine. Thus, the nearest meaning is (A).

questions.stem:
Choose the word opposite in meaning to the word given below:

**FRAGILE**
questions.solution: “Fragile” means easily broken or damaged; “sturdy” means strong and solid. Thus, they are opposites.

questions.stem:
Arrange P, Q, R and S to form a coherent five-sentence paragraph, with sentence 1 first.

1. In 1854, physician John Snow began investigating a cholera outbreak in London's Soho district.
P. He marked each reported death on a street map.
Q. The resulting cluster centred on a public water pump in Broad Street.
R. This pattern challenged the prevailing belief that cholera spread chiefly through foul air.
S. Snow persuaded local officials to remove the pump handle, though the outbreak was already waning.
questions.solution: P introduces the map, Q describes the cluster it revealed, R explains the significance of the pattern, and S gives Snow’s subsequent response. Thus, the coherent order is PQRS.

questions.stem: Although the rebuttal was ___, its single sentence pinpointed the flaw in a lengthy argument.
questions.solution: “Laconic” means brief or using few words, fitting a single-sentence rebuttal to a lengthy argument.

questions.stem:
Arrange the parts P, Q, R and S to form a coherent paragraph.

P: Neha checks her timetable for the next day's classes.
Q: It tells her which books and notebooks she will need.
R: She places those items in her schoolbag.
S: The bag is ready beside the door, so she can leave promptly in the morning.

Which is the correct sequence?
questions.solution: P introduces the timetable, which Q explains tells Neha what books and notebooks she needs. R describes packing those items, and S concludes with the ready bag.

questions.stem:
Choose the word nearest in meaning to the word given below:

BRIEF
questions.solution: “Brief” means short in duration or length.

questions.stem: Choose the best replacement for the underlined part of the sentence: The agency introduced the revised procedure <u>with a view to reduce processing delays and improving accountability</u> across its regional offices.

options.text: with a view to reduce processing delays and improving accountability
with a view to reducing processing delays and improving accountability
with a view to reducing processing delays and to improve accountability
with a view to reduce processing delays and improve accountability

questions.solution: In “with a view to,” the word “to” is a preposition and is followed by gerunds. The parallel forms are “reducing” and “improving.”

questions.stem: The rain had soaked our clothes, so we were _____ when the café owner offered us towels.
questions.solution: “Grateful” means thankful; after being soaked, we would appreciate the owner’s offer of towels.

questions.stem: My younger brother is very fond _____ solving jigsaw puzzles in his free time.
questions.solution: The standard expression is “fond of,” followed by a gerund: “fond of solving.”

questions.stem:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error.
(A) The clerk
(B) has stamped the parcel
(C) yesterday
(D) before the post office closed.
questions.solution: “Yesterday” indicates a completed past time, so the simple past is required: “has stamped” should be “stamped.”

questions.stem: The regulator asked its inspectors to ___ allegations of concealed payments by tracing each transfer and interviewing witnesses.
questions.solution: “Look into” means to investigate, which matches tracing transfers and interviewing witnesses.

questions.stem:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions that follow.

Urban trees are often praised for making streets attractive, but their most important benefits are practical. A mature canopy shades pavements and buildings, reducing the amount of heat absorbed during the day. Trees also release water vapour, which can cool the surrounding air. Together, these effects can make a neighbourhood more comfortable during hot weather and reduce the need for some indoor cooling.

These benefits, however, are not distributed evenly. Some districts have broad, continuous canopies, while others have few trees and extensive paved surfaces. Residents of the latter areas may face greater heat exposure, especially when they have limited access to cooled indoor spaces. Planting programmes can help address this imbalance, but counting saplings alone is a poor measure of success. Young trees may not survive without adequate watering, suitable soil, and protection from damage; even healthy saplings take years to provide substantial shade.

Effective urban forestry therefore requires both careful placement and long-term maintenance. Local residents can help planners identify streets where shade is most needed, while city agencies must ensure that newly planted trees receive continued care. Trees cannot replace other measures, such as well-designed buildings or reliable public services during heat waves. Still, when integrated into broader planning, a healthy urban canopy can make cities cooler and more equitable.

What is the central idea of the passage?

options.text: Urban trees are chiefly valuable because they improve the appearance of city streets.
Tree-planting programmes should replace other measures used to manage urban heat.
Urban trees can reduce heat, but their benefits depend on fair placement and sustained care.
Mature trees are the only practical way for cities to provide residents with cooling.

questions.solution: The passage explains that trees reduce urban heat, but their benefits are uneven unless trees are placed where shade is needed and maintained over time. They complement, rather than replace, other heat-management measures.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about a city that reports planting many saplings but does not track their survival?

options.text: Its residents will receive immediate cooling because saplings release water vapour.
Its planting total may overstate the lasting shade and cooling the programme will provide.
Its hottest districts will necessarily gain the greatest number of mature trees.
Its tree programme will reduce the need for reliable public services during heat waves.

questions.solution: Saplings may not survive, and young trees take years to provide substantial shade. Therefore, planting totals may overstate the programme’s lasting shade and cooling benefits.

questions.stem: Three pairs show a specialist and the work the specialist produces. Which pair is wrongly grouped?
questions.solution: A novelist writes a novel, a cartographer produces a map, and a composer creates a symphony. A conductor leads an orchestra rather than producing it, so this pair is wrongly grouped.

questions.stem: Which word cannot be formed using the letters of “counterrevolutionaries”, without using any letter more often than it occurs in that word?
questions.solution: The word “counterrevolutionaries” contains no $y$, whereas “uncertainty” requires one. Hence “uncertainty” cannot be formed.

questions.stem:
**Statements:**
All painters are artists.
Some artists are sculptors.

**Conclusions:**
I. Some painters are sculptors.
II. Some artists are sculptors.
questions.solution: Conclusion I does not follow, since the artists who are sculptors need not be painters. Conclusion II follows directly from the second statement.

questions.stem: Select the number pair related to the given pair in the same way: $18 : 81 :: 23 : ?$
questions.solution:
The rule is to square the sum of the digits: $(1+8)^2=81$.
$$ (2+3)^2=25 $$

questions.stem: One term in the following $\alpha-numeric$ series is wrong. Identify it: D-3, I-4, H-8, M-10, L-15, Q-18, P-24, U-27.
questions.solution:
The odd-position numbers increase by $+5,+7,+9$: $3,8,15,24$. The even-position numbers increase by $+6,+8,+10$: $4,10,18,28$.
Thus the last term should be $U$-$28$, so $U$-$27$ is incorrect.

questions.solution: Three of the figures are rotations of the same figure; figure (A) is its mirror image, which cannot be obtained by rotation.

questions.stem: In a certain code, **LAMP** is written as **NCOR**. How will **FROG** be written in the same code?
questions.solution: Each letter is shifted forward by 2 places in the alphabet. Thus, $F\to H$, $R\to T$, $O\to Q$, and $G\to I$, giving $\boxed{HTQI}$.

questions.stem: Mira, a woman, points to a man and says, “He is the son of the only daughter of my maternal grandmother.” How is Mira related to him?
questions.solution: The only daughter of Mira’s maternal grandmother is Mira’s mother. The man is her mother’s son, so he is Mira’s brother; hence Mira is his sister.

questions.stem: Find the missing number in the given figure.
questions.solution: In each row, the third number is the product of the first two: 5, 6 → 30; 9, 9 → 81. So, 4, 8 → 32.

questions.solution: In a mirror image the figure is inverted left to right; top and bottom remain unchanged. Only option (B) shows this.

questions.stem: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^\pi \dfrac{x\sin x}{1+\cos^2 x}\,dx$.
questions.solution:
Let $f(x)=\dfrac{\sin x}{1+\cos^2 x}$. Since $f(\pi-x)=f(x)$,
$$\int_0^\pi xf(x)\,dx=\frac{\pi}{2}\int_0^\pi f(x)\,dx.$$
Using $u=\cos x$, $\displaystyle\int_0^\pi f(x)\,dx=\int_{-1}^1\frac{du}{1+u^2}=\frac{\pi}{2}$. Hence the value is $\boxed{\dfrac{\pi^2}{4}}$.

questions.stem: The focus of the parabola $y^2=-16x$ is
questions.solution:
Comparing with the standard form $y^2=4ax$, we get $4a=-16$, so $a=-4$.
The focus is $(a,0)=(-4,0)$.

questions.stem: The image of the point $(3,2)$ in the line $2x+3y+1=0$ is
questions.solution:
For reflection across $ax+by+c=0$, the image of $(x_1,y_1)$ is $(x_1,y_1)-\dfrac{2(ax_1+by_1+c)}{a^2+b^2}(a,b)$. Thus
$$ (3,2)-\frac{2(13)}{13}(2,3)=(-1,-4). $$

questions.stem: The range of $f(x)=\dfrac{2x+1}{x^2+2}$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$, is
questions.solution:
Let $y=\dfrac{2x+1}{x^2+2}$. Then $yx^2-2x+(2y-1)=0$ must have a real root in $x$.
$$\Delta=4-4y(2y-1)\ge0\iff(2y+1)(y-1)\le0$$
Hence $-\dfrac12\le y\le1$; both endpoints are attained at $x=-2$ and $x=1$, respectively.

questions.stem: For positive integers $n,k$, the term independent of $x$ in $(x+\dfrac{1}{x^k})^n$ is the fifth term with coefficient $495$. Find $n+k$.
questions.solution:
The general term is $T_{r+1}=\binom{n}{r}x^{n-(k+1)r}$. Since the constant term is the fifth term, $r=4$ and $\binom{n}{4}=495$, giving $n=12$.
For the term to be independent of $x$, $12-4(k+1)=0$, so $k=2$. Hence $n+k=14$.

questions.stem: For $x>0$, the general solution of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+\dfrac{2x+1}{x(x+1)}y=\dfrac{1}{x^2+1}$ is:
questions.solution:
The integrating factor is $e^{\int(1/x+1/(x+1))\,dx}=x(x+1)$. Hence
$$[x(x+1)y]'=\frac{x(x+1)}{x^2+1}=1+\frac{x-1}{x^2+1}.$$
Integrating and dividing by $x(x+1)$ gives $y=\dfrac{x+\frac12\ln(x^2+1)-\tan^{-1}x+C}{x(x+1)}$, option (B).

questions.stem: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^\pi \dfrac{1+\cos x}{2+\sin x}\,dx$ using $t=\tan\dfrac{x}{2}$.
questions.solution:
Using $t=\tan\dfrac{x}{2}$, we have $\sin x=\dfrac{2t}{1+t^2}$, $1+\cos x=\dfrac{2}{1+t^2}$, and $dx=\dfrac{2\,dt}{1+t^2}$.
$$I=2\int_0^\infty\frac{dt}{(1+t^2)(t^2+t+1)}$$
Since $\dfrac{1}{(1+t^2)(t^2+t+1)}=-\dfrac{t}{1+t^2}+\dfrac{t+1}{t^2+t+1}$, the logarithmic boundary term vanishes, giving $I=\int_0^\infty\dfrac{dt}{t^2+t+1}=\dfrac{2\pi}{3\sqrt{3}}$.

questions.stem: If $A$ is a $3\times3$ matrix with $|A|=-2$, find $|\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A)|+|A\operatorname{adj}A|$.
questions.solution:
For a $3\times3$ matrix $M$, $|\operatorname{adj}M|=|M|^2$. Thus $|\operatorname{adj}A|=(-2)^2=4$, so $|\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A)|=4^2=16$.
Also, $|A\operatorname{adj}A|=|A||\operatorname{adj}A|=(-2)(4)=-8$.
Hence the required sum is $16-8=8$.

questions.stem: The sum of the first $n$ terms of $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}\dfrac{1}{k(k+2)}$ is
questions.solution:
Using partial fractions, $\frac{1}{k(k+2)}=\frac12\bigl(\frac1k-\frac1{k+2}\bigr)$, so the sum telescopes:
$$S_n=\frac12\biggl(1+\frac12-\frac1{n+1}-\frac1{n+2}\biggr)=\frac{n(3n+5)}{4(n+1)(n+2)}.$$

questions.stem: The general solution of $5\cos x-12\sin x=\dfrac{13}{2}$ is
questions.solution:
Write $5\cos x-12\sin x=13\cos(x+\alpha)$, where $\alpha=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{12}{5}\right)$. Thus
$$\cos(x+\alpha)=\frac12\implies x+\alpha=2n\pi\pm\frac{\pi}{3},\quad n\in\mathbb Z.$$
Hence $x=2n\pi-\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{12}{5}\right)\pm\frac{\pi}{3}$.

questions.stem: If $5\cos\theta+12\sin\theta=7$, evaluate $\dfrac{-119\cos 2\theta+120\sin 2\theta}{5\cos\theta+12\sin\theta}$.
questions.solution:
Let $U=5\cos\theta+12\sin\theta$ and $V=12\cos\theta-5\sin\theta$. Then $U^2+V^2=169$ and $U^2-V^2=-119\cos 2\theta+120\sin 2\theta$.
Since $U=7$, the numerator is $2U^2-169=2(49)-169=-71$; hence the required value is $\dfrac{-71}{7}$.

questions.stem: Let $[\vec p,\vec q,\vec r]=\vec p\cdot(\vec q\times\vec r)$. If $[\vec a,\vec b,\vec c]=2$, $[\vec a,\vec b,\vec d]=5$, $[\vec a,\vec c,\vec d]=-3$, and $[\vec b,\vec c,\vec d]=4$, find $[\vec a+\vec b,\vec b+\vec c,\vec c+\vec d]$.
questions.solution:
By trilinearity and the vanishing of terms with repeated vectors,
$$[\vec a+\vec b,\vec b+\vec c,\vec c+\vec d]=[\vec a,\vec b,\vec c]+[\vec a,\vec b,\vec d]+[\vec a,\vec c,\vec d]+[\vec b,\vec c,\vec d]=2+5-3+4=8.$$

questions.stem: The curve $x^2+xy+y^2=7$ passes through $(1,2)$. What is the equation of its tangent at that point?
questions.solution:
For $F(x,y)=x^2+xy+y^2-7$, the tangent at $(1,2)$ is given by $F_x(x-1)+F_y(y-2)=0$. Since $(F_x,F_y)=(2x+y,x+2y)=(4,5)$ there,
$$4(x-1)+5(y-2)=0\implies 4x+5y-14=0.$$

questions.stem: For the lines $\dfrac{x}{1}=\dfrac{y}{1}=\dfrac{z}{1}$ and $\dfrac{x-1}{1}=\dfrac{y}{-1}=\dfrac{z}{1}$, which is the correct relation and shortest distance?
questions.solution:
The direction vectors are $\vec u=(1,1,1)$ and $\vec v=(1,-1,1)$. Since $\vec u\times\vec v=(2,0,-2)$ and $(1,0,0)\cdot(\vec u\times\vec v)=2\ne0$, the lines are skew.
$$d=\frac{|(1,0,0)\cdot(\vec u\times\vec v)|}{|\vec u\times\vec v|}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{8}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.$$

questions.stem: The differential equation corresponding to the family $y=a(x-b)^3$, where $a$ and $b$ are arbitrary constants, is
questions.solution:
Differentiating $y=a(x-b)^3$ gives $y'=3a(x-b)^2$ and $y''=6a(x-b)$. Hence
$$3yy''=18a^2(x-b)^4=2(y')^2.$$

questions.stem: The absolute maximum value of $f(x)=x^3-3x^2-9x+4$ on $[-2,2]$ is
questions.solution:
For an absolute maximum on a closed interval, check the endpoints and critical points. Since $f'(x)=3(x-3)(x+1)$, the only critical point in $[-2,2]$ is $x=-1$.
$$f(-2)=2,\quad f(-1)=9,\quad f(2)=-18$$
Hence the absolute maximum value is $9$.

questions.stem: For which values of $a$ is $f(x)=e^x(x^2+ax+2)$ strictly increasing on $[-2,2]$?
questions.solution:
$f'(x)=e^xq(x)$, where $q(x)=x^2+(a+2)x+(a+2)$. Since $e^x>0$, it suffices that $q(x)\ge0$ on $[-2,2]$; its minimum there is nonnegative exactly when $0\le a+2\le4$.
Thus $-2\le a\le2$. The derivative can vanish only at isolated points, so $f$ is strictly increasing throughout this interval.

questions.stem: For what values of $k$ do both roots of $x^2-\dfrac{3}{2}x+k=0$ lie in $(0,1)$?
questions.solution:
For roots $r_1,r_2$, their product is $k$ and $(1-r_1)(1-r_2)=k-\frac12$. Both roots are positive and less than $1$ when $k>\frac12$; real roots also require $\Delta=\frac94-4k\ge0$.
Thus $\frac12<k\le\frac9{16}$.

questions.stem: For what value of $\lambda$ does the system $x+y+z=1,\quad 2x-y+z=2,\quad 3x+\bigl(2+\lambda(\lambda-1)\bigr)z=3+\lambda$ have infinitely many solutions?
questions.solution:
Adding the first two equations gives $3x+2z=3$. For infinitely many solutions, the third equation must be dependent on this equation, so its coefficients and constant must match:
$$\lambda(\lambda-1)=0,\qquad 3+\lambda=3.$$
The second condition gives $\lambda=0$, which also satisfies the first.

questions.stem: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\sqrt{3}} x\arctan x\,dx$.
questions.solution:
Using integration by parts, take $u=\arctan x$ and $dv=x\,dx$:
$$I=\left[\frac{x^2}{2}\arctan x\right]_0^{\sqrt3}-\frac12\int_0^{\sqrt3}\frac{x^2}{1+x^2}\,dx
=\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac12\left(\sqrt3-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)
=\frac{2\pi}{3}-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}.$$

questions.stem: The value of the repeating decimal $0.\overline{27}$, viewed as the sum of an infinite geometric series, is
questions.solution:
The repeating decimal is a geometric series with first term $\dfrac{27}{100}$ and common ratio $\dfrac{1}{100}$.
$$S=\frac{27/100}{1-1/100}=\frac{27}{99}=\frac{3}{11}$$

questions.stem: The number of onto functions from a set with $6$ elements to a set with $4$ elements is
questions.solution:
By inclusion–exclusion, subtract functions missing at least one codomain element:
$$N=4^6-\binom41 3^6+\binom42 2^6-\binom43 1^6=4096-2916+384-4=1560.$$

questions.stem: For what value of $\lambda$ are the points with position vectors $\vec a=\hat i+2\hat j$, $\vec b=3\hat i+\hat j+2\hat k$ and $\vec c=5\hat i+\lambda\hat j+4\hat k$ collinear?
questions.solution:
For collinearity, the vectors $\vec b-\vec a$ and $\vec c-\vec a$ must be proportional.
$$\vec b-\vec a=(2,-1,2),\qquad \vec c-\vec a=(4,\lambda-2,4)=2(\vec b-\vec a)$$
Thus $\lambda-2=-2$, giving $\lambda=0$.

questions.stem: How many five-digit numbers formed from $0,1,2,3,4,5$ without repetition have $2$ and $3$ adjacent?
questions.solution:
If $0$ is used, choose the other two digits in $\binom{3}{2}$ ways. Arranging the adjacent pair in either order, excluding arrangements with leading zero, gives $\binom{3}{2}(2\cdot4!-2\cdot3!)=108$.
If $0$ is omitted, the pair acts as one block, so the count is $2\cdot4!=48$.
$$108+48=156$$

questions.stem: For $x,y\ge0$ and $x+y\le1$, simplify $\sin^{-1}x+\sin^{-1}y$ to a single inverse sine.
questions.solution:
Let $\alpha=\sin^{-1}x$ and $\beta=\sin^{-1}y$. Since $x+y\le1$, we have $\alpha+\beta\le\frac{\pi}{2}$, so $\sin^{-1}(\sin(\alpha+\beta))=\alpha+\beta$.
$$\sin(\alpha+\beta)=x\sqrt{1-y^2}+y\sqrt{1-x^2}$$
Hence the sum is $\sin^{-1}\!\left(x\sqrt{1-y^2}+y\sqrt{1-x^2}\right)$.

questions.stem: Which pair of compound propositions is logically equivalent for every truth assignment to $p,q,r$?
questions.solution:
Using $a\Rightarrow b\equiv\sim a\vee b$,
$$[\sim(p\wedge q)]\Rightarrow r\equiv(p\wedge q)\vee r.$$
Also, $\sim[(p\Rightarrow\sim q)\wedge\sim r]\equiv\sim[(\sim p\vee\sim q)\wedge\sim r]\equiv(p\wedge q)\vee r$; hence the pair in (D) is equivalent.

questions.stem: The area enclosed by the parabola $x=y^2$ and the line $x=y+2$ is
questions.solution:
The curves intersect at $y^2=y+2$, giving $y=-1,2$. Hence,
$$A=\int_{-1}^{2}(y+2-y^2)\,dy=\left[\frac{y^2}{2}+2y-\frac{y^3}{3}\right]_{-1}^{2}=\frac{9}{2}$$
square units.

An ellipse is centred at $(2,-1)$, has foci $(-1,-1)$ and $(5,-1)$, and passes through $(2,3)$. Its equation is
questions.solution:
The foci are $3$ units from the centre, so $c=3$. Since $(2,3)$ is $4$ units vertically from the centre, $b=4$; hence $a^2=b^2+c^2=16+9=25$.
$$\frac{(x-2)^2}{25}+\frac{(y+1)^2}{16}=1$$

questions.stem: Find the equation of the circle passing through $(1,2)$, $(4,1)$ and $(2,5)$.
questions.solution:
Let the circle be $x^2+y^2+Dx+Ey+F=0$. Substituting the three points gives $3D-E=-12$, $D+3E=-24$, hence $D=E=-6$ and $F=13$.
Therefore, $x^2+y^2-6x-6y+13=0$.

questions.stem: A committee of $3$ is selected from $8$ people, including P and Q. How many committees have at least one of P and Q absent?
questions.solution:
A committee fails the condition only if it contains both P and Q. Thus,
$$\binom{8}{3}-\binom{6}{1}=56-6=50.$$

questions.stem: Machines A, B and C supply $\frac{1}{2}$, $\frac{1}{3}$ and $\frac{1}{6}$ of a factory's components; their defect rates are $2\%$, $4\%$ and $9\%$. Given a component is defective, find the probability it came from B.
Let $f(x)=ax^2+bx$ for $x<1$ and $f(x)=\ln x+2$ for $x\geq 1$. If $f$ is differentiable at $x=1$, find $(a,b)$.
questions.solution:
Differentiability at $x=1$ requires continuity and equality of the one-sided derivatives:
$$a+b=\ln 1+2=2,\qquad 2a+b=\left.\frac{d}{dx}(\ln x+2)\right|_{x=1}=1.$$
Solving gives $a=-1$ and $b=3$, so $(a,b)=(-1,3)$.

questions.stem: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1 \dfrac{2x}{1+x^2}\,dx$.
questions.solution:
Let $t=1+x^2$, so $dt=2x\,dx$. Then
$$\int_0^1 \frac{2x}{1+x^2}\,dx=\int_1^2 \frac{dt}{t}=\ln 2.$$

questions.stem: In a survey of 72 people, everyone uses at least one of three apps. The numbers using A, B and C are 42, 38 and 35; the pairwise intersection sizes are 18, 16 and 15. How many use exactly two apps?
questions.solution:
By inclusion–exclusion, the number using all three apps is
$$n(A\cap B\cap C)=72-(42+38+35)+(18+16+15)=6.$$
The pairwise intersections count each person using all three three times, so exactly two apps are used by $(18+16+15)-3(6)=31$ people.

questions.stem: For a complex number $z$, if $|z-(11+4i)|=2|z-(5+4i)|$, the maximum value of $|z|$ is
questions.solution:
Let $z=x+iy$. The given locus is
$$
(x-11)^2+(y-4)^2=4[(x-5)^2+(y-4)^2]\Rightarrow (x-3)^2+(y-4)^2=16.
$$
This circle has centre $(3,4)$ and radius $4$, so the maximum distance from the origin is $\sqrt{3^2+4^2}+4=9$.

questions.stem: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$, which is such that $A^2=2A+3I$, find the $(1,2)$ entry of $A^8$.
questions.solution: From $A^2=2A+3I$, the characteristic roots are $24$.

questions.stem: The domain of $f(x)=\sqrt{5-2x}$ is
questions.solution:
For the square root to be defined, $5-2x\ge 0$.
$$x\le\frac{5}{2}$$
Hence the domain is $\left(-\infty,\frac{5}{2}\right]$.

questions.stem: A data set has mean $4$ and variance $9$. If each observation $x_i$ is replaced by $y_i=2x_i+3$, the new mean and variance are
questions.solution:
For a linear transformation $y_i=ax_i+b$, $\bar y=a\bar x+b$ and $\operatorname{Var}(y)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(x)$. Thus
$$\bar y=2(4)+3=11,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(y)=2^2(9)=36.$$

questions.stem: A random variable $X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,p)$ has mean $4$ and satisfies $P(X=3)=2P(X=2)$. Find $P(X=4)$.
questions.solution:
For $X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,p)$, $np=4$ and $\dfrac{P(X=3)}{P(X=2)}=\dfrac{n-2}{3}\dfrac{p}{1-p}=2$. Using $np=4$ gives $p=\dfrac12$, hence $n=8$.
$$P(X=4)=\binom84\left(\frac12\right)^8=\frac{35}{128}.$$

questions.stem: Two cards are drawn without replacement from a standard $52$-card deck. What is the probability that at least one is an ace or a king?
questions.solution:
Among the 52 cards, 44 are neither aces nor kings. Using the complement,
$$P=1-\frac{\binom{44}{2}}{\binom{52}{2}}=1-\frac{946}{1326}=\frac{190}{663}.$$

questions.stem: If the lines $x=1+u,\ y=-2+2u,\ z=3+3u$ and $x=p+2v,\ y=1-v,\ z=-1+v$ intersect, then $p$ equals
questions.solution:
For two non-parallel lines to intersect, they must be coplanar: $(B-A)\cdot(\mathbf d_1\times\mathbf d_2)=0$.
$$\mathbf d_1\times\mathbf d_2=(1,2,3)\times(2,-1,1)=(5,5,-5)$$
With $B-A=(p-1,3,-4)$, $(p-1,3,-4)\cdot(5,5,-5)=0$, giving $5(p-1)+15+20=0$.
Hence $p=-6$.

questions.stem: Evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{1-\cos(4x)}{\sin(2x)\tan(3x)}$.
questions.solution:
Using $1-\cos t\sim \frac{t^2}{2}$, $\sin t\sim t$ and $\tan t\sim t$ as $t\to0$,
$$\lim_{x\to0}\frac{1-\cos(4x)}{\sin(2x)\tan(3x)}=\frac{(4x)^2/2}{(2x)(3x)}=\frac{4}{3}.$$

questions.stem: The line through the intersection of $2x+y-3=0$ and $x-y-3=0$, perpendicular to $2x-3y+5=0$, is
questions.solution:
Solving the two equations gives their intersection $(2,-1)$. The given line has slope $\frac{2}{3}$, so the required perpendicular slope is $-\frac{3}{2}$.
$$y+1=-\frac{3}{2}(x-2)\quad\Rightarrow\quad 3x+2y-4=0$$
